role: Processing worker at a coffee estate's wet mill
headline: Back in the hills of Pu'er after vocational school, a coffee processing worker who started out weighing cherries at a coffee estate's processing station, and every harvest follows the fruit through flotation, pulping, fermentation and drying
unit: A coffee estate with its own processing plant in the hills of Simao district, Pu'er, Yunnan (three hundred mu of its own coffee, about twenty hectares, buying cherries from nearby farmers too, with a small roasting room)
level: You've picked coffee in your family's plot since you were small and can tell ripe red cherries from green at a glance. You roughly know what washed and natural processing mean, but the acidity of the fermentation tank and the moisture content on the drying beds you still need the old hand to teach you
intro: The winter you finished vocational school, you came back to Pu'er. At the door of the processing station the estate owner handed you a pair of rubber boots and a straw hat, pointed at an electronic scale and said: the harvest is here, start by learning to weigh. The mist hadn't lifted from the valley, and the first people with bamboo baskets on their backs were already coming down from the coffee plots. As of today, every red cherry picked on this hillside passes through your hands first.
salary_note: Estimate: at a coffee estate in the Pu'er hills, the harvest (November to March) brings lots of overtime and piece rates, and the off-season pays base wage only, with meals and lodging; averaged over the year it's a notch below the national figure. As a cupper or technical supervisor, at an estate whose specialty beans sell well, the pay is good for Pu'er.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Cupping coffee and judging its aroma and mouthfeel

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Sorting green coffee and removing defective beans

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related job listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: Outside the estate dorm window there's nothing but mist; across the valley you can only make out a few big trees on the far ridge. You pull on your boots and get a bowl of rice noodles from the canteen, with a spoonful of pickled greens.

Receiving cherries. The pickers queue with their bamboo baskets; you tip the cherries into a crate, weigh them, and grab a handful to see how much is ripe red, docking weight where there's too much green. One woman says every cherry from her family was picked one by one. You smile, and dock a little anyway.

Flotation. The cherries go into the water channel, and the shriveled and insect-bored ones float up for you to scoop away with a net. The ones that sink flow on into the pulper, and the skins pile up to one side; dried, they sell as cascara tea.

By the fermentation tank you test the acidity with a meter, check the temperature, and note it all down square by square on a clipboard. The old hand grabs a fistful of beans, rubs them, and says six more hours; only when they stop feeling slippery can they be washed.

The drying yard. Row after row of raised beds spread with beans, and you go along turning each one with a wooden rake, every two hours. The sun is fierce, and under the straw hat sweat runs into your eyes; you squeeze a handful of beans and listen to the sound they make.

Clouds come rolling over the ridge. The owner shouts once over the walkie-talkie and everyone drops what they're doing and runs for the drying yard, pulling tarpaulins over bed after bed; as the last one is covered, the rain is already hammering down.

In the roasting room, the old hand is roasting a batch for tourists. You stand beside him listening; the first crack sounds like popcorn, and watching the curve on the screen, he tells you to write down the temperature at that moment.
Before going back to the dorm you take one more look at the fermentation tank by torchlight, fine bubbles rising on the surface. The hills are very quiet, only dogs barking in a village far off.

ladder.title: Coffee Processing Hand
ladder.focus: At harvest, weigh in cherries, float, pulp, ferment and turn the beans on the drying beds; in the off-season repair the drying racks and clean the warehouse. You get your own step of the process on quick hands, hard work, and being able to read how dry the beans are.

ladder.title: Coffee Processing Worker, Level 4
ladder.focus: Handle the hulling, grading, optical sorting and hand-sorting of parchment coffee, and learn roast curves, roasted beans and drip bags. You move up on low defect rates and steady roasting.

ladder.title: Processing Station Team Leader
ladder.focus: At harvest, run a processing line of a dozen people: the rota, the batches for fermentation and drying, dealing with the farmers who bring cherries, guarding against mold and rain. You move up on consistent batches, low losses and holding the team together.

ladder.title: Quality Control Cupper
ladder.focus: Cup and score every lot, set its grade and price, send samples to buyers and discuss quality, and feed the cupping results back into processing. You move up on accurate scores and buyers who trust you.

ladder.title: Plant Technical Supervisor
ladder.focus: Run the whole plant's processing methods, trials of new varieties and new processes, equipment purchasing and certification audits, and lead the cuppers and team leaders. You hold the job on the reputation and price of the estate's beans.

ai_tasks.name: Sorting green coffee and removing defective beans
ai_tasks.how: Camera-equipped optical sorters and machine vision can spot and reject beans with abnormal color or shape automatically. A person only checks regularly for defects missed and good beans wrongly rejected.

ai_tasks.name: Weighing and loading green coffee for roasting
ai_tasks.how: Automatic weighing and loading systems dose to the recipe, and AI or the system records batches and quantities. A person only tops up supplies, clears jams and spot-checks.

ai_tasks.name: Running the roaster and monitoring roast temperature and time
ai_tasks.how: Sensors and AI can log the temperature curve in real time, warn of anomalies and control the heat within set limits. When the beans are unusual or the machine misbehaves, someone still has to judge and step in on the spot.

ai_tasks.name: Adjusting roast curves and other processing parameters
ai_tasks.how: AI can recommend curves and fine-tune parameters from past batches, helping reproduce stable results. What flavor you're after, and which direction to take each coffee, is still a person's call.

ai_tasks.name: Grinding coffee to order and adjusting the grind size
ai_tasks.how: Grinders grind automatically to the set particle size, and AI can recommend a grind for each brewing method. A person only calibrates the first batch and spot-checks.

ai_tasks.name: Cupping coffee and judging its aroma and mouthfeel
ai_tasks.how: Cupping depends on a person's smell and taste to perceive aroma, acidity and mouthfeel, and on experience to judge good from bad. AI can only help organize score sheets and compare them with past batches.

ai_tasks.name: Testing moisture, color and other quality indicators
ai_tasks.how: Moisture meters and colorimeters measure automatically, and AI logs the readings, compares them with the standard and flags batches out of spec. A person calibrates the instruments and deals with abnormal results.

ai_tasks.name: Cleaning and maintaining roasters, grinders and other equipment
ai_tasks.how: AI can schedule maintenance and predict faults from operating data. The cleaning, taking apart and replacing parts is still hands-on work for a person.

events.e_rain_loss: A night rain came too fast, and the beds you were responsible for didn't get covered in time and were soaked through. The next day the owner took one look and said those beds could only be sold as a lower grade. He didn't shout, but for days afterwards you turned the beans with particular care.
events.e_first_cup: The old hand took you cupping for the first time. A row of bowls of ground coffee, hot water poured on; you copied him, breaking the crust of grounds with a spoon, leaning in to smell, then slurping. You tasted a sourness a bit like yangmei, the Chinese bayberry, and he said: yes, that's our hillside.
events.e_sun: A whole harvest of turning beans in the drying yard peeled a layer of skin off your neck and the backs of your hands. Your mother brought down a jar of herbal salve she'd boiled up herself in the village.
events.e_price_up: International coffee prices shot up, and the price paid for fresh cherries more than doubled. The farmers bringing cherries were all smiles, and your father phoned to say the family's few mu of coffee had finally stopped losing money this year.
events.e_mold: In the rainy season the warehouse turned damp, and a few sacks of parchment coffee from one lot grew patches of mold. You and the old hand opened every sack, smelled it and looked bean by bean; everything picked out was burned, and that lot's account came up a long way short.
events.e_love: A young woman from Kunming came to the estate to run coffee tours and brought tourists through the processing station. She asked you to explain fermentation; you stumbled through it, and she said you did it better than the script she'd memorized.
events.e_sorter: The plant bought an optical sorter that can look at hundreds of beans a second and blow out the wrong-colored ones in one puff. The women at the hand-sorting tables went from eight to three, and the ones who stayed pick out only the few defects the machine can't recognize.
events.e_frost: One winter a rare frost came, and overnight a great swathe of leaves on the low-lying coffee trees turned black. You went out to the plots with the owner, and he crouched under one tree for a long time without saying anything. That harvest brought in thirty percent fewer cherries.
events.e_buyer_visit: The owner of a specialty coffee shop in Shanghai came to the estate to look at beans and stood in the processing station all day, asking you how many hours each lot fermented and how many days it dried. When he left he ordered two tonnes, saying he wanted the honey-process lot.
events.e_wedding: You got married, and the village feasted for three days. The estate owner sent over a bag of a lot you'd processed yourself, roasted, in a bag printed with both your names.
events.e_curve_soft: The roasting room installed software that stores every batch's temperature curve and can control the heat automatically to match the best one. You cupped its recommended curves side by side with your own roasts; two you couldn't tell apart, and one it roasted flat.
events.e_child: Your child was born at the busiest point of the harvest. You stayed two days at the hospital and went back to the processing station, and in the evenings on video the baby's little hands grabbed at the screen.
events.e_price_down: Coffee prices fell back again, and the cherry price halved in a year. Some families in the hills cut down their coffee to plant something else. Your father asked whether you should cut a few mu too. You said wait a bit.
events.e_contest: A lot of anaerobic natural you processed made the top ten in the province's green coffee competition and was bought at auction by an overseas buyer. A banner went up at the estate gate, and your mother came down from the village specially to see it.
events.e_back: Shouldering dozens of sacks of parchment a day at harvest, your back finally gave out; once you bent down you couldn't get up. You lay in the dorm for a week and handed the processing line to your apprentice.
events.e_house: You put down a deposit on a flat in Simao town, where your child will go to school. At harvest you live at the estate; in the off-season you drive forty minutes of mountain road home every day.
events.e_new_variety: The owner tried a few dozen trees of a new variety on the slope, and three years later they fruited for the first time. You picked them one by one, processed and dried them separately, and on cupping day the whole estate crowded at the cupping room door.
events.e_apprentice: The new lad never turned the beans all the way to the bottom, and the lowest layer went musty. You didn't scold him; you had him push his hand down into the beans with yours, and when he felt the warmth at the bottom, he understood.
events.e_parents: Your father fell in the plot and hurt his leg. It was the height of the harvest; by day you were at the processing station and at night you went back to the village to pick for your family, and for over a month you never slept through.
events.e_old_buyer: The owner of that Shanghai coffee shop came again, his hair half white. He took a bag of beans from his bag and said it was the lot you processed ten years ago; he'd kept a little and cupped it once every year.
events.e_young_leave: One by one the young people from the village went to Kunming, to Guangdong, and the women who came to pick got older and older. The owner says in a few years the cherries on the hill will need machines to pick them, but on slopes like these, no machine can get up.
events.e_eyes: Picking defects at the hand-sorting table, you found you had to hold the beans further away to see them. You got a pair of reading glasses and hung them on the cupping room wall.

c_anaerobic.title: Learn special processing or not
c_anaerobic.situation: The owner wants to try anaerobic fermentation and honey processing to sell to specialty coffee shops in the cities. A lot has to be watched for days and nights, with acidity, sugar and temperature tested every few hours and all the data entered on a tablet. The old hand says plain washed is fine, and all that fuss might not even sell.

options.label: Learn with the owner
options.result: You kept watch by the fermentation tank for three nights straight, filling the tablet's grid square by square. The first anaerobic lot cupped with a red-wine note; some said good, some said strange, and the owner said it would sell.

options.label: Stick with washed, like the old hand
options.result: You stayed on the washed line, pulping, fermenting and washing lot after lot. The beans came out clean and consistent, and the buying station said your washed coffee could be taken without inspection.

c_cert.title: Sit the Level 4 Coffee Processing Worker certificate
c_cert.situation: The prefecture's vocational skills testing station has started a coffee processing exam. With the Level 4 certificate the plant pays ¥200 more a month, and it counts later for running the dry mill. The exam means memorizing coffee grading standards and food safety, and the practical tests hulling and roasting.

options.label: Sit it
options.result: You memorized the grading standards in the dorm at night, which screen size and how many defects make which grade, until you dreamed of beans. On the day of the practical you roasted a light-medium batch; the examiner smelled it and passed you.

options.label: Skip it, rely on your hands
options.result: You spent the time at the hand-sorting table, looking bean by bean for defects. No certificate, but when the old hand was away, the owner had you cover the hulling for him.

c_shanghai.title: Go to a roasting plant in Shanghai
c_shanghai.situation: The Shanghai coffee company that came to look at beans is hiring roasters, saying people who know the origin can roast something different. They offer more than double what you earn now, with lodging, only you'd get back to Pu'er once or twice a year.

options.label: Go to Shanghai
options.result: At the Shanghai roasting plant you roast beans from Ethiopia, Colombia and Yunnan every day. One day you came to a sack from Pu'er, opened it, took one smell, and knew which hillside it came from.

options.label: Stay in the hills
options.result: You turned it down. That night you sat a while in the drying yard, looking at the lights of the village on the hill opposite.

c_lead.title: Go for Processing Station Team Leader
c_lead.situation: The team leader of the washed line has gone home to open a shop, the harvest is almost here, and the owner will pick someone from the plant to run the line: a dozen people's rota, every lot's fermentation and drying, dealing with the farmers who bring cherries. The other candidate is older than you, and the farmers all know him.

options.label: Go for it
options.result: You turned years of fermentation times and drying days from your notebook into a table and showed the owner. He let you try it for one harvest, and the other man later became your deputy.

options.label: Let him have it
options.result: He became team leader and you ran the fermentation tanks. He dealt with the farmers and you watched the acidity and temperature, and that harvest's beans were cleaner than any year before.

c_own.title: Go back to the village and do it yourself
c_own.situation: Your father says the family's dozen or so mu of coffee, plus your relatives', is enough for a small processing station. A coffee friend in Kunming is also calling you, wanting to open a roasting studio together that sells only Yunnan beans. The owner hears about it and offers you a raise.

options.label: Build a station in the village
options.result: Behind your family's courtyard you built fermentation tanks and put up drying beds. In a harvest you process only twenty-odd tonnes of your relatives' cherries, and every lot is labeled with whose plot it came from.
options.end: You built a small processing station in the village for your own family's and your relatives' cherries; every sack of beans says which slope it came from and which day it was picked.

options.label: Open a roasting studio in Kunming
options.result: You rented a little shop on an old street in Kunming, with one small roaster and photos of the Pu'er hills on the wall. When customers ask where you're from, you say: where these beans grow.
options.end: You opened a small roasting studio in Kunming that sells only Yunnan beans; every harvest you go back to the Pu'er hills for a month to process a lot.

options.label: Stay for the raise
options.result: You stayed. The owner hung a sign at the door of the processing station saying who runs this line.

c_q.title: Get a cupping certificate and move to quality control
c_q.situation: The owner wants you to sit an internationally recognized coffee grading certificate, and if you pass, move over as quality control cupper, scoring and pricing every lot. Training and exams mean a month in Kunming; the owner pays half, and if you fail, the rest is on you.

options.label: Sit it
options.result: In the training room in Kunming you smelled aroma vials and tasted hundreds of cups for a month, sour, bitter, over-fermented. You failed one module the first time and passed the resit.

options.label: Don't
options.result: You said you still like being on the processing line. The owner brought in a cupper from outside, who often comes to ask you how a lot was processed after he's scored it.

c_grade.title: How hard to grade
c_grade.situation: Prices have fallen, and the owner wants to mark the cherries he's bought down a grade or so to pay farmers a little less. Among the people bringing cherries are ones you've called aunt and uncle since you were small, and the scores on the cupping sheet are yours.

options.label: Score it straight
options.result: You graded by the cupping results: good cherries, good price. The owner had a few words with you in a meeting, but the next year everyone in the village brought their best cherries here.

options.label: Do as the owner says
options.result: You pushed the scores on the sheet down a few points. That harvest the accounts looked good, and when you went back to the village, one aunt saw you and didn't say hello.

c_teach.title: Teach part-time at the vocational school
c_teach.situation: A vocational school in Pu'er has started a coffee course and is missing someone who's come out of a processing station. They ask you to teach two afternoons of practicals a week, from cherry processing to cupping. It's the busy harvest, so if you go you'll be making up the work at the estate at night.

options.label: Teach part-time
options.result: In the school's little processing station you take a group of seventeen- and eighteen-year-olds through flotation, turning the beans and cupping, and like your old teacher did, you have them push their hands down into the beans. Two of the students came to the estate after graduating.

options.label: Don't go
options.result: You said you couldn't get away at harvest. The school found someone else, and when that teacher brought students to visit the estate, he asked you to talk to them for a quarter of an hour in the drying yard.

c_chief.title: Plant Technical Supervisor or not
c_chief.situation: The estate has grown, and the owner wants one person to run the whole plant's methods: trials of new varieties, new processes, equipment purchasing and buyers' certification audits. You'd be in the office and in meetings year-round, with half your cupping time gone.

options.label: Take it
options.result: Every day you read the processing line's data, negotiate prices with equipment makers, and walk buyers' auditors through the station. Every lot made with a new process, you still cup yourself before it goes out.

options.label: Put your apprentice forward
options.result: You pushed up the apprentice you'd trained and kept the cupping room yourself. Whatever beans he's unsure of, he carries over to you.

endings.retire: The day your last harvest ended, you still went to the processing station in the morning to look at the cherries coming in, grabbing a handful to see how much was red. In the afternoon you went to the cupping room, poured hot water over a row of bowls one last time, broke the crust of grounds and leaned in to smell. You tasted a sourness a bit like yangmei, said nothing, and wrote the score on the cupping sheet.
endings.burnout: That harvest your back gave out for good; once you bent over in the drying yard you couldn't straighten up again, and your apprentice helped you back to the dorm. You only heard half of what the doctor said. You told the owner you were done and went back to the village. When the harvest comes round, you still go out to your family's plot every afternoon to see if the cherries are red yet.

stages: At harvest you follow the cherries all the way through: weighing them in each morning, checking how much is red and docking where there's too much green; scooping floaters from the flotation channel and making sure the pulper doesn't jam; testing acidity by the fermentation tank and noting it on the clipboard; turning the beans bed by bed in the drying yard with a wooden rake in the afternoon. The picking women know the cherries better than you, the old hand knows the sky better than you, and you have to listen to both.

Parchment coffee is yours now: through the huller, the grading screens, the density table and the optical sorter one after another, with three women at the hand-sorting table following you to pick out the defects the machine can't see. Every day you test moisture content with the meter, and weigh and label each lot before it goes into the warehouse. In the evenings you go to the roasting room and roast a batch to a curve in the software, then cup it the next day yourself and note in your book where this batch fell short of the last.

At harvest a processing line of a dozen people is yours: the morning rota, who receives cherries, who watches the tanks, who goes to the drying yard; farmers bringing cherries haggle with you, and when the fruit is poor you have to say so to their faces. Every lot's fermentation time and drying days are your call, and so is shouting for everyone to bring the beans in ten minutes before the rain. In the off-season you repair the pulper, replace the drying nets, and put the year's lot records into tables.

Every lot has to pass through your cupping room: grind, pour, break the crust, slurp, score, describe the flavor, grade it, price it. When coffee companies in Shanghai or Guangzhou ask for samples, you send them off bag by bag, then phone each one to explain why this lot got this score. When a cupping comes out wrong, you take the sheet back to the processing line and work out with the team leader whether it was the fermentation or the drying.

You run the whole plant's methods: which plot trials a new variety this year, which cherries get which process, you write the plan. When equipment makers come pushing new machines, you read the specs and negotiate the price; when buyers' certification auditors come, you walk them from receiving to the warehouse. Once a week you meet the cuppers and team leaders, and you still go to the cupping room every day, only now you sit at the end.
work: One woman's cherries have a lot of green mixed in; she says her grandson helped pick. You don't make her sort them again; you crouch by the crate and pick them out yourself one by one, weigh her share, and pour her a bowl of water.

The pulper jams, cherries piling up and spilling out of the hopper. You switch it off, reach in and pull out a tangle of twigs wrapped round the rollers, and the old hand says from behind you: next time, check the flotation channel has been scooped clean first.
On the twelfth day of drying you grab a handful of beans and shake them in your hand, and the sound has turned crisp. The moisture meter reads 11.5, and the old hand nods: this bed can come in.

Among the beans the optical sorter blows out, you notice a pale yellow kind of good bean being rejected too. You turn down the sensitivity a little and have the women at the hand-sorting table go through that tub again.

A tourist wants a pound of dark roast for cold brew. You pick a lot from the warehouse heavy on chocolate notes, drop it just as the second crack starts, and brew yourself a cup to taste before you bag it.
Passing through the grading screens, the size 16 screen has a small hole in it, and lots of small beans get through. You stop to change the screen and run those few sacks through again.

On the busiest day of the harvest, more than forty farmers turn up with cherries at once. You split receiving in two, one point to weigh and one to inspect, put your apprentice on the scale, and stand at the inspection point yourself, looking at crate after crate.

The forecast says rain in three days, and a dozen beds in the drying yard still aren't dry. You have the wettest few moved into the covered drying house and add two people to turn the beans through the night.

An old farmer says you pay less than the buying station and wants to take his cherries away. You ask him to sit down and show him the cupping score and sale price of his family's lot from last year; he thinks a while, then unloads his cherries.

A washed lot cups with an over-fermented boozy note, and you mark it down a grade on the sheet. The next day you check the records on the processing line: that tank was left to soak eight hours longer than the others.

A coffee company in Guangzhou says the sample you sent doesn't match the bulk shipment. You take out the retained sample and cup it again; it scores only half a point off the bulk, and you write a very long email with both cupping sheets attached.

The new quality control assistant always scores high. You have him cup a row of ten bowls at the same time as you, then put both sets of scores side by side and go through, cup by cup, why yours is two points lower.

An equipment maker is pushing a new fermentation tank that controls temperature and logs data automatically. You have him lend you one to trial for a harvest, process the same lot in it and in the old tank side by side, and sign the contract only after cupping both.

An overseas buyer's certification auditor comes and wants to see which plot every lot comes from. You walk him from the coffee plots to receiving, the fermentation tanks, the drying yard and the warehouse, opening the logbook at every stop.

In the third year the new variety on the slope bears fruit, you decide to split it three ways: washed, natural and anaerobic. On cupping day you have the whole plant come and taste, and in the end decide which one to plant more of next year.
past: You grew up in a village in the hills of Pu'er. Your grandfather grew tea all his life; in the years around your birth your father turned half the tea plot over to coffee, saying people in the cities had started drinking it.

Every winter you went to the plot with your family to pick coffee, only the red cherries, one by one. The cherries were sold to the buying station, and in those years the price was low, and your father always said coffee wasn't as good as tea.

You didn't get into the county high school after the entrance exam, and went to vocational school in Simao to study agricultural product processing. The teachers taught tea and fruit; coffee got one lesson.
On your vocational placement you were sent to a coffee buying station. Everything there was bought mixed together, good and bad at one price, and for the first time you felt it was a bit of a waste.

A coffee maker from out of province stayed in the village for two weeks and brewed you a cup of your family's coffee with a little pour-over kettle. You tasted a fruity sweetness and couldn't believe it came from your own plot.

Before graduating you heard a new estate had opened over the ridge, doing specialty beans and processing its own. You rode over an hour on a motorbike to find the owner; he asked if you could pick cherries, and you said you'd known how since you were small.

late.pension_note: Estimate: Yunnan's urban employee pension scheme. The estate paid in on the minimum base in the early years, with gaps in the off-season, so in retirement you get about 40% of your last monthly salary; the family coffee plot still brings in a little each year.
scenes: The first harvest after you retire, you still wake very early every morning and open the window, listening for whether the pulper at the station over the ridge has started up.
The estate asks you back for a month every harvest. You don't work the line; you just sit in the cupping room, and when the young ones finish scoring, they pass you the sheet to glance at.

You take your grandson to pick coffee in the family plot and teach him to pick only the red ones. He picks a handful of green; you say nothing, pick out the green ones, and put them in your own pocket.

For the first few months back in the village, your back hurt too much to go into the plot. You sat in the courtyard watching the coffee trees on the slope turn red bit by bit, anxious, and unable to go and pick.

Once your back was a bit better, you roasted a batch of your family's beans in an iron wok in the courtyard, the way your grandfather used to fire tea. It came out uneven; you took a sip and said it still tasted of that hillside.

An old colleague from the estate came to see you and said the station has fully automatic fermentation tanks and drying houses now, and no one has to run when it rains anymore. You asked if they still turn the beans. Yes, he said, the machines do.
The first harvest after leaving the estate, every afternoon you'd look at the sky, and when you saw clouds rolling over the ridge your hands would reach for a tarpaulin without thinking.

An apprentice you trained has become a team leader, and sends you a photo of the drying yard, the beans on the beds spread very evenly, captioned: like my teacher said, hand all the way to the bottom.
A coffee shop menu in the city reads "Pu'er, Yunnan · Anaerobic Natural." You order a cup, taste a hint of red wine, and think of those three nights.

Lots of processing stations use optical sorters and automatic fermentation tanks now, and roasting follows curves in the software. But which bed of beans is ready to come in, which cup has fermented too far, still needs a person to feel and to taste.

Your back and wrists ache in the rainy season, from shouldering and turning beans when you were young. When the harvest comes, you still walk the slope every morning to see whether this year's cherries are ripening evenly.

A few young people have come back to the village and opened guesthouses and cafés on the hill, telling visitors from the city how coffee goes from cherry to bean. You listen at the door for a while and think they don't do a bad job.

closing.retire: One misty morning in the hills many years later, you brew yourself a cup of coffee in the courtyard, taste a sourness a bit like yangmei, and remember what the old hand said: that's our hillside.
closing.burnout: Many years later, you sit on a bamboo chair in the village, listening to the machines running at the processing station down the slope. Your granddaughter runs up and asks why coffee beans have to dry for so many days. They have to finish saying what they have to say, you tell her.
closing.end: Many years later, sorting through old things, you find the clipboard filled with fermentation times and drying days, its pages once soaked by rain, the writing still legible. You hang it on the wall, beside your grandfather's old straw hat.
